# Cascade (01, engineer) — SPD-086

## Brief
`hooks/pathrule.glob_to_regex` reads `[` as the start of a character class, exactly as a shell
glob does. A deliverable naming a Next.js dynamic route segment therefore matches no real path:
`admin/src/app/accounts/[email]/**` compiles to a class over `e`, `m`, `a`, `i`, `l`, so the only
paths it can match are ones with a single letter where the directory name belongs. The effect is
that an agent is silently read-only on the exact files it owns: BADS-054/Snowden was refused
`admin/src/app/accounts/[email]/page.tsx` with "Law 5: ... is not among BADS-054/Snowden's
deliverables (admin/src/app/accounts/[email]/**)" -- its own planned glob quoted back at it. There
is already a member row in the ledger carrying that glob. Reproduce first:

    from spudlib.hooks.pathrule import path_matches_glob as m
    p = 'admin/src/app/accounts/[email]/_components/UserTab.tsx'
    m(p, 'admin/src/app/accounts/[email]/**')   # False, the bug
    m(p, 'admin/src/app/accounts/?email?/**')   # True
    m(p, 'admin/src/app/accounts/**')           # True

Choosing the fix is the work. The ticket names two candidates and neither is free:

1. Escape the metacharacters. Note two obstacles the ticket found and one it did not. The shell
   spelling `[[]email[]]` does not survive `glob_to_regex` either: the `[]]` branch finds its
   closing `]` at the first character, emits an empty class, and the regex that comes out is
   malformed rather than literal. And a backslash escape cannot reach the matcher at all, because
   `state/ops.normalize_bare_deliverable` does `.replace("\\", "/")` on every deliverable, so
   `\[email\]` is stored as `/[email/]`. An escape therefore needs work on both sides, and it
   leaves the caller responsible for knowing a spelling nobody currently writes.
2. Literal prefix when a glob has no wildcard outside a trailing `/**`. Narrower, but decide what
   counts as a wildcard: if `[` does not count, `tests/test_hooks.py`'s existing
   `match("a/b?c", "a/b[?]c")` case changes meaning; if it does count, the Next.js glob is not
   fixed.

Consider a third, which I think is the strongest and which you should accept or refute with
evidence rather than assume: **a bracket is always literal in a deliverable glob** -- drop
character-class support from `glob_to_regex` entirely and emit `re.escape` for `[` and `]`. The
argument: deliverable globs are written by Spud and by parents, never by a shell; a character
class in one is essentially never intended, while a literal bracket is routine in any Next.js
tree; the only class in the whole repository is that one test case; and it removes the failure
mode rather than adding a warning about it. The argument against is that it silently changes the
meaning of any glob that did mean a class. Weigh it, pick one, and say in your Result why.

The ticket also asks that `member new` refuse or at least warn about a deliverable glob that can
match no path under the project, since the current failure is silent until an agent is mid-run and
blames its own brief. Read that request critically: as literally stated it is wrong, because a
member planned to *create* `bin/spudlib/hooks/newmod.py` legitimately matches nothing that exists
yet, and refusing that would break ordinary planning. Decide what the honest check is -- and note
that if brackets become literal there may be no ambiguity left to warn about, in which case say so
instead of adding a check that earns nothing. If you do add one, it must not walk the checkout on
every plan and must not refuse a glob for a file that does not exist yet.

`pathrule` is on the hook path, so time the change with the probe below; a hook change passes
within 1 ms of main.

Pin the result with tests: the three `path_matches_glob` cases above, a `member new` planning a
deliverable that names a `[segment]` directory with a write inside it allowed by the edit hook
(end to end through the hook, not only the matcher), whatever you decide about the malformed
`[]]` spelling, and the existing `test_glob_semantics` case updated or kept deliberately, never
deleted to make a suite pass.

## Result
A bracket is now a literal character in a deliverable glob. bin/spudlib/hooks/pathrule.py: deleted the character-class branch from glob_to_regex (every character but *, ? and ** is re.escape'd), with the decision and its evidence in a comment above the function; bin/spudlib/state/ops.py: normalize_deliverable's docstring states the glob language; bin/spudlib/cli/helptexts.py: a 'deliverable globs' section in the root EPILOG, which spud --help renders. Chose option 3 over the other two on evidence: of every member ever planned, the only globs holding a bracket are BAD-054's three, all three a literal Next.js segment (one the ?email? workaround this bug forced); no class is documented anywhere and SPUD_PATHS holds none, so the only class in the repository was the test case a/b[?]c. Class support was also unsafe on the hook path -- the shell escape [[]email[]] compiled to an unterminated set, so path_matches_glob raised re.PatternError inside PreToolUse, which fails closed; with brackets literal glob_to_regex is total. Option 1 is refused by the code on both sides (the escape spellings do not survive glob_to_regex, and normalize_bare_deliverable folds a backslash into a slash before storage) and still leaves every parent owing a spelling nobody writes; option 2 fixes only the trailing-/** shape, leaving [email]/*.tsx and [id]/**/*.test.ts broken, and its definition of a wildcard either breaks a/b[?]c or fails to fix the Next.js glob. The member new check the ticket asked for: not added, deliberately. As stated it refuses a member planned to create a file that does not exist yet; it would have to walk a checkout that may not be there; and with brackets literal there is nothing left to warn about, because every glob normalize_deliverable accepts matches some path -- every character is a wildcard or a literal, and .., absolute paths and empty segments are already refused. Tests in tests/test_hooks.py: test_glob_semantics keeps its a/b[?]c case with the meaning changed deliberately (a literal bracket pair around the one-character wildcard: a/b[x]c matches, a/b?c no longer does); test_brackets_are_literal pins the three cases from the brief, the Next.js catch-all and optional catch-all routes, and that [[]..[]], []], a bare [ and the class-shaped [!x] and [a-z] each name themselves instead of raising; test_no_accepted_glob_is_unsatisfiable builds a witness path for fifteen glob shapes; and PreEditTest.test_a_bracketed_segment_is_a_directory_the_hook_lets_its_member_write runs BAD-054's own plan and writes end to end through member new and the PreToolUse edit hook, for Write, Edit and MultiEdit, with the refusals for the paths the character class used to match. Verified: full suite 876 tests OK in 631s, no bytecode left; hook_timing.py 30 rounds against main is within 0.25 ms on every hook case (Bash -0.01, Write +0.23, SessionStart -0.17, Stop +0.08); module_sizes puts pathrule at 256 and ops at 250, both a net removal of code plus documentation, no split warranted. Left for Spud: CLAUDE.md's Commands section still says 873 tests and is his file, not mine; and the existing BAD-054 rows keep their ?email? workaround glob, which still matches (pinned by a test), so nothing has to be re-planned.

## Outcome
Chose the strongest of the three candidates and argued it from the ledger: every bracket glob ever planned names a literal segment, no class is documented anywhere, and the class branch was itself unsafe on the hook path, where the shell's own escape raised re.PatternError inside a fail-closed PreToolUse. Declined the member new check the ticket asked for, correctly: it would refuse a member planned to create a file that does not exist yet, and with brackets literal there is nothing left to warn about, pinned by a witness test rather than asserted.
